issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Ravi was sixty-four years old, a warehouse worker who had spent most of his life stacking pallets and driving forklifts in a sprawling distribution center on the outskirts of Chicago. He was married to his wife, Sunita, for thirty-eight years, and they had raised two children who were now grown and living on the East Coast. But the man who came to the clinic was barely recognizable as the same person Sunita had known for decades. He had not been the same since the three days he spent held captive in a shipping container behind an abandoned truck stop outside of Delhi during a visit to his homeland.

The kidnapping happened at 2 a.m. on a sweltering July night. Ravi had been waiting for a bus back to his village when a van pulled up, and two men yanked him inside. They blindfolded him and drove for hours before shoving him into a dark, metal container. For three days, he was kept in total blackness, the heat suffocating, and the only sound was the rustle of something slithering across the floor. He never saw the snake, but he heard it at night, and he felt a cold, scaled body brush against his ankle on the second night. He had been certain he would die either from the snake or from the heat or from the men who occasionally slid water under the door but never spoke. When he was finally released-left on a roadside with nothing but his soiled clothes-he had not told his family the full story. He said he had been robbed and lost his wallet. But the truth of that container stayed locked inside him, and it began to leak out in ways he could not control.

Back in Chicago, Ravi tried to return to work, but the warehouse became a minefield. The night shift, which he had worked for years, now terrified him. He started requesting day shifts, but even then, the dimly lit aisles of stacked boxes made his heart pound. He found himself constantly looking over his shoulder while walking the warehouse floor, convinced that someone was following him-though he knew logically no one was. The most puzzling trigger was snakes. A coworker once left a book on reptiles in the break room, and Ravi had a full-blown panic attack. He could not explain why, but the image of a snake's coil sent him back into that container. He began avoiding any conversation about animals, and if someone so much as mentioned a snake, he would walk away.

Nighttime became unbearable. He could not bring himself to go to sleep at the same hour the kidnapping had occurred-2 a.m.-so he stayed awake until exhaustion forced him to collapse. Even then, he could only sleep with the lights on. The dark felt like a physical presence, pressing on his chest, and he would wake up drenched in sweat, gasping. Sunita found herself waking repeatedly to his restless thrashing and his repeated questions: "Am I okay? Am I safe? Check my ankles-is there a mark?" She would inspect his skin, find nothing, and tell him he was fine, but he would ask again an hour later. He checked his own body constantly throughout the day-running his hands over his arms, his legs, his stomach-searching for any sting or bite or bruise that might signal that danger had finally found him.

The consequences began to pile up. He missed work three times in one month due to exhaustion, and his supervisor warned him that he was on probation. Sunita grew short with him, snapping that she could not keep telling him he was safe when nothing was actually wrong. He stopped going out after sunset altogether, which meant no dinners with friends, no evening walks, no visits to his grandson's school plays. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally helpless-that no matter what he did, bad things would happen to him. Some nights, lying rigidly in bed, he thought that maybe life was not worth living anymore. He never said it aloud, but the thought sat in his chest like a stone. He also avoided thinking about the event at all, because he was certain that if he let his mind go there, he would fall apart completely and never recover.

What finally brought Ravi to the clinic was a confrontation with Sunita. She had found him at 3 a.m. standing in the kitchen, staring at the knife block, and she demanded that he get help or she would leave. He made an appointment the next morning. In the waiting room, he sat with his back to the wall, scanning the room for exits. He did not know if therapy could help-he was afraid that talking about the event would destroy him-but he was also afraid of losing Sunita, of losing his job, of losing himself. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could tell him he was safe and that he could finally trust it.
